title: Kabuliwala
significance: A brief bond between a peddler from Kabul and a girl in Calcutta overlays the time of a stranger with the time of a father. Written for a magazine as part of the story cycle of the 1890s, it is the most widely read of those pieces and shows the process by which the Bengali short story took shape as a form.

title: Gitanjali
significance: The Bengali original appeared in 1910, and the selection Tagore translated into English himself and published in London in 1912 became the basis for the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature. The English volume does not share the same contents as the original and converts its fixed meter into the tone of prose, so the two versions read, in effect, as different books.

title: Gora
significance: A young man who has been an ardent defender of Hindu orthodoxy learns the truth of his own birth, and the novel takes the debate itself as its narrative, addressing how religion, caste, and nation harden into a single person's identity. It is the largest in scale of Tagore's novels.

title: The Post Office
significance: A nearly one-act play in which a sick child confined to a room waits for a letter that never comes, sustaining the stage on nothing but the time of waiting rather than incident. Among Tagore's plays, it is the one most often staged, in the most languages.

title: The Home and the World
significance: A landowner, his wife, and a Swadeshi activist narrate in turn, each in the first person, setting three moral calculations of the same events side by side. It is a rare novel that interrogates the violence inside the anticolonial movement from within the movement rather than from outside it.

title: Nationalism
significance: An English-language essay collection gathering lectures he delivered in Japan and the United States, it criticizes empire while at the same time questioning the nation-state as a form, even the nation-state that opposes empire. It is a text that shows a colonial intellectual could hold independence as a goal without making the nation its object.

title: I Am a Cat
significance: A serialized work that sets up a nameless cat as narrator to observe Meiji intellectual society, it was Soseki's debut in the literary world. His prose — capable of drawing on classical Chinese allusion and the spoken rhythm of rakugo within a single sentence — appears here for the first time in finished form.

title: Botchan
significance: It narrates, in a fast-moving first-person colloquial voice, the missteps of a Tokyo-born teacher posted to a provincial middle school. It draws on Soseki's own experience teaching in Shikoku and remains the most widely read modern novel in Japan.

title: Theory of Literature
significance: A theoretical work organizing his reading during his years of study in London together with his lectures at Tokyo Imperial University, it tried to explain how literature works as a combination — expressed as (F+f) — of cognition and feeling. As an attempt to establish principles for literature in general without borrowing the evaluative standards of English literature, it is the starting point of Soseki's criticism.

title: Sanshiro
significance: A bildungsroman in which a first-year university student newly arrived from Kyushu passes in turn through the scholarship, romance, and class structure of Tokyo, it is the first volume of the so-called early trilogy. It stands for the period when the Asahi Shimbun serialized novel became literature's central form.

title: And Then
significance: A man who does not work and lives on his family's money chooses again the woman he had once ceded to a friend, and loses his livelihood and social standing together. It is the work in which Soseki most coldly calculates a structure in which an individual's ethical choice becomes, at the same time, economic ruin.

title: Kokoro
significance: In a three-part structure that joins a young man's recollections to Sensei's long suicide letter, it belatedly discloses the calculations of a man who carried the memory of betraying a friend for his whole life. By linking the death of the Meiji Emperor and General Nogi Maresuke's ritual suicide to one man's decision, it translates the end of an era into private guilt.

title: A Madman's Diary
significance: Published in New Youth, it was China's first serious vernacular-language short story, taking a double structure in which a classical-Chinese preface encloses a diary written in the vernacular. It sets up a narrator who reads the record of Confucian morality as a document that eats people, interrogating the legitimacy of tradition itself through the form of the narration. It was collected in 1923 in his first story collection, Outcry.

title: The True Story of Ah Q
significance: A novella serialized in a newspaper supplement from December 1921 to February of the following year, it coined the diagnosis of the spiritual victory method through Ah Q, a day laborer who remembers being beaten as having won. It is a rare case in which a character's name became a common noun for a society's self-perception, and it was collected in 1923 in Outcry.

title: A Brief History of Chinese Fiction
significance: A general history compiled from his lectures at Peking University, it was the first work to arrange zhiguai tales, chuanqi tales, huaben, and vernacular novels — all of them outside the classical-Chinese orthodoxy — into a single lineage. It established fiction, long held in contempt, as an object of scholarship, and it became the basic framework for the study of Chinese fiction history thereafter.

title: Wandering
significance: His second story collection, gathering pieces including New Year's Sacrifice, The Loner, and Regret for the Past. Written in the place left behind once the slogans of enlightenment had cleared away, it treats the powerlessness of intellectuals and the deaths of women, and shows the point where the combative tone of Outcry turns into self-doubt.

title: Wild Grass
significance: His only poetry collection, gathering prose poems he had published scattered across magazines from 1924 onward, it pushes self-negation forward through images such as dreams, shadows, and epitaphs. It is the most formally experimental of Lu Xun's works and belongs to neither fiction nor the zawen.

title: Old Tales Retold
significance: His last story collection, it rewrites ancient figures and myths — the Great Yu, Boyi and Shuqi, Mozi, Laozi — while deliberately mixing in modern speech and scenes. It uses the collision of anachronism, rather than quotation, as its method for dismantling the authority of the classics.

title: Rashomon
significance: Taking only the plot from a short episode in the Konjaku Monogatarishu, it compresses into a scene of a few minutes a servant's decision between starving to death and becoming a thief. It is the work in which Akutagawa's method of using a classical tale as a testing ground for modern psychology first reaches finished form.

title: The Nose
significance: A monk ashamed of his long nose finds himself mocked all the more once it shortens, a single incident that exposes the resentment people feel when another's misfortune is relieved. Natsume Soseki's high praise soon after its publication became Akutagawa's entry point into the literary world.

title: Hell Screen
significance: The story of a painter who has to watch his own daughter burn in order to paint a screen depicting hell, it pushes to an extreme the price the completion of art demands. Its narration, which conveys the event solely through a witness's recollection, is distinctive for leaving the painter's inner life empty to the end.

title: In a Grove
significance: It does nothing but line up, in turn, the statements of those involved in a single murder, and never rules on which is true. The structure makes the reliability of narration the novel's subject, and it left behind an idiom for the state of not being able to tell whose account is correct.

title: Kappa
significance: A satire in the form of a travelogue told by a mental-hospital patient recounting what he experienced in the land of the kappa, it depicts a society in which the institutions of childbirth, labor, and art have all been turned upside down. It is an early instance, within modern Japanese literature, of using a speculative setting as a device for social criticism.

title: Spinning Gears
significance: A late work recording, in six disconnected sections, a disintegrating set of sensations that begins with translucent gears appearing in his field of vision; it was published posthumously in the year of his suicide. It shows the final phase in which he abandoned his early method of reconstructing classical tales and made himself the object under observation.

title: Geonchuk Muhan Yukmyeongakche
significance: A sequence published in Japanese in the house journal of the Joseon Architectural Association, it pulled mathematical formulas, geometric terminology, and advertising copy into its lines of verse. It is an early work that shows Yi Sang's experiments, known to readers as Korean-language poetry, in fact began first on the printed page of a Japanese-language journal.

title: Ogamdo
significance: A poem sequence published in a newspaper's literary column, it pushed lines stripped of spacing, number grids, and mirror-reversed type onto the printed page exactly as they were. The very fact that reader protest halted the serialization after fifteen poems left, as a matter of record, the limit that formal experiment ran into in modern Korean poetry.

title: Wings
significance: It records a day in the life of a narrator who lives on money his wife earns and spends his time inside a room. The opening aphorism and the narrative that follows are arranged to betray each other, presenting the incapacity of the colonial intellectual as structure rather than explanation.

title: Jongsaenggi
significance: A late work that takes the form of writing an account of one's own death in advance, overlaying the boundaries between narrator, author, and character, it was published posthumously in the year he died in Tokyo. It stands at the far end of a direction in which fiction is written not as story but as a commentary on one's own sentences.

title: Gwontae
significance: An essay observing a day on which nothing happens while staying in the countryside in summer, it was published in a newspaper after his death. Because Yi Sang's characteristic sense of time is sustained even in plain sentences stripped of experimental notation, it serves as an entry point for understanding his prose.

title: Azaleas
significance: The only poetry collection he published in his lifetime, it carries most of his representative poems along with the title piece. It carried the three-beat meter and 7-5 syllable pattern of folk song over into the line breaks of printed free verse, fixing the tone of a speaker enduring separation as the standard register of Korean lyric poetry.

title: Chohon
significance: Taking as its form the procedure, in traditional funeral rites, of calling out the name of the dead, it uses repetition to build a structure in which the call never finally reaches its object. Among the poems collected in Azaleas, it is among the most intense in its tone of loss.

title: Sanyuhwa
significance: It describes flowers blooming and falling on a mountain exactly as they are, with no human story attached, showing that Sowol's poetry can stand on detached observation and not only on the outpouring of feeling. It builds the cycle of the seasons from nothing more than short lines and repetition.

title: Sihon
significance: An essay on poetics published in the magazine Gaebyeok, it argues that the worth of a poem lies not in the scale of its subject matter but in the depth of its 'soul,' formulating the principles of his own poetry in his own words. It is the only substantial piece of criticism Sowol left behind.

title: Sowol Sicho
significance: A selected-poems volume compiled after Sowol's death by his teacher Kim Eok, it gathered together poems that had been published separately, scattered across magazines. It is an edition that shows through whose hands the Sowol canon was assembled after his death.

title: Joseon Bulgyo Yusinnon
significance: An essay that critiques Korean Buddhism item by item — education, ritual, clerical marriage, temple administration — and proposes reforms for each. A work that addresses modern institutional problems in the language of religious reform, it shows the logic of Manhae's thought before it moved into poetry.

title: Bulgyo Daejeon
significance: A compilation that draws passages from the vast body of Buddhist scripture and rearranges them by theme, it reorganized scripture as a text that could be read and quoted rather than only an object of faith. It is a source that shows where the paradoxical syntax of Nimui Chimmuk came from.

title: Joseon Dongnibui Seo
significance: An essay written in prison after his arrest for the March 1st Movement, it argues the legitimacy of independence on the grounds of freedom and peace. It is a case in which the condition of standing in for a courtroom statement determined the structure of the prose, and it is the most tightly argued of Manhae's prose writings.

title: Nimui Chimmuk
significance: A sequence collection in which the entire volume continues as speech addressed to 'nim.' Thanks to a design that never settles 'nim' into any one of lover, Buddha, or a lost sovereignty, love song, religious poetry, and political utterance could share the same sentence under censorship.

title: Sevasadan
significance: The title means 'the house of service.' His first Hindi-language novel, it connects the question of where the institution of marriage and the dowry system push women with the problem of urban prostitution; separate Urdu and Hindi versions of the work exist.

title: Rangbhoomi
significance: The title means 'battlefield.' The story of a blind beggar who defends his land to the end against its seizure for a factory site, it is Premchand's largest novel in scale, narrating industrialization and land dispossession narrowed down to one man's resistance.

title: The Shroud
significance: While a daughter-in-law lies dying in childbirth, a father and son sit outside roasting potatoes, then spend on drink the money collected for her shroud. A late story stripped entirely of moral commentary, it shows how far his early, enlightenment-minded tone had traveled.

title: Godan
significance: The title means 'the donation of a cow.' His last completed novel, it narrates, set to the cycle of the seasons, how Hori, a tenant farmer who only wanted to own a cow, is destroyed by debt, fines, and customary expenses; it remains the standard text of the Indian village novel.

title: Sahitya ka Uddeshya
significance: His presidential address to the founding conference of the All India Progressive Writers' Association, it defined literature not as entertainment or ornament but as a measure for judging reality. Delivered a few months before his death, it became the programmatic document of India's later progressive literature.
